s: How many freedoms are presently guaranteed under Article 19(1) of the Constitution of India?
x: Article 19(1) presently guarantees six freedoms. Originally, it contained seven freedoms, but the freedom relating to property was deleted.
tq: Use the numerical change from seven original freedoms to six present freedoms.
sec: Article 19(1) clauses (a) to (g), deleted clause (f), freedoms not listed, Articles 19-22  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following is correctly matched with the corresponding provision of Article 19(1)?
o: Clause (e) — Freedom of speech and expression
Clause (c) — Freedom to move freely throughout India
Clause (b) — Freedom to form associations or unions
Clause (d) — Freedom to move freely throughout India
x: Article 19(1)(d) guarantees the freedom to move freely throughout the territory of India. Clause (b) concerns peaceful assembly, clause (c) concerns associations, and clause (e) concerns residence and settlement.
tq: Discriminate between neighbouring Article 19 clauses by matching each clause with its exact freedom.
sec: Article 19(1) clauses (a) to (g), deleted clause (f), freedoms not listed, Articles 19-22  [APPSC]

s: The freedom to reside and settle in any part of India is guaranteed under:
x: Article 19(1)(e) guarantees citizens the freedom to reside and settle in any part of India.
tq: Test the exact clause number attached to a specific freedom.
sec: Article 19(1) clauses (a) to (g), deleted clause (f), freedoms not listed, Articles 19-22  [APPSC]

s: Which of the following freedoms is guaranteed under Article 19(1)(g)?
o: Freedom to assemble peaceably and without arms
Freedom to reside and settle in any part of India
Freedom to practise any profession or carry on any occupation, trade or business
x: Article 19(1)(g) guarantees the freedom to practise any profession or to carry on any occupation, trade or business.
tq: Match the occupational freedom with its precise constitutional clause.
sec: Article 19(1) clauses (a) to (g), deleted clause (f), freedoms not listed, Articles 19-22  [APPSC]

s:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 19(1)(c):
1. It includes the right to form associations or unions.
2. The reference to co-operative societies was added by the 97th Constitutional Amendment.
3. It originally included the right to acquire, hold and dispose of property.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The right to acquire, hold and dispose of property belonged to Article 19(1)(f), not Article 19(1)(c), and was later deleted.
tq: Separate the original property clause from the association clause and identify the amendment-added phrase.
sec: Article 19(1) clauses (a) to (g), deleted clause (f), freedoms not listed, Articles 19-22  [APPSC]

s: The freedom to acquire, hold and dispose of property was deleted from Article 19(1) by the:
x: The 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 deleted Article 19(1)(f), which had guaranteed the freedom to acquire, hold and dispose of property.
tq: Distinguish the amendment that deleted the property freedom from other major constitutional amendments.
sec: Article 19(1) clauses (a) to (g), deleted clause (f), freedoms not listed, Articles 19-22  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following is NOT included among the six freedoms presently guaranteed by Article 19(1)?
o: Freedom to carry on any occupation, trade or business
Freedom to move freely throughout India
Freedom to acquire, hold and dispose of property
x: The freedom to acquire, hold and dispose of property was Article 19(1)(f), but it was deleted by the 44th Amendment in 1978. The other three are among the six present freedoms.
tq: Find the deleted clause rather than selecting one of the six surviving freedoms.
sec: Article 19(1) clauses (a) to (g), deleted clause (f), freedoms not listed, Articles 19-22  [APPSC]

s: The group of Fundamental Rights known as the Right to Freedom is contained in:
x: The Right to Freedom comprises Articles 19 to 22 of the Constitution.
tq: Identify the constitutional range associated with a named group of Fundamental Rights.
sec: Article 19(1) clauses (a) to (g), deleted clause (f), freedoms not listed, Articles 19-22  [APPSC]

s: Freedom of expression under Article 19(1)(a) came into force on:
x: The freedom of expression under Article 19(1)(a) was in force from 26 January 1950, when the Constitution commenced.
tq: Distinguish the Constitution’s adoption date from its commencement date.
sec: Article 19(1) clauses (a) to (g), deleted clause (f), freedoms not listed, Articles 19-22  [APPSC]

s: Which of the following is not expressly enumerated in Article 19(1), but has been recognised by judicial interpretation as part of freedom of speech and expression?
o: Right to acquire property under Article 19(1)(f)
Right to strike as a Fundamental Right
Freedom to travel abroad under Article 19(1)(d)
x: Freedom of the press is not separately listed in Article 19(1), but courts have read it into freedom of speech and expression. There is no Fundamental Right to strike, travel abroad is associated with Article 21, and Article 19(1)(f) has been deleted.
tq: Separate judicially implied freedoms from rights expressly listed or specifically excluded.
sec: Article 19(1) clauses (a) to (g), deleted clause (f), freedoms not listed, Articles 19-22  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
x: The right to information has been read into Article 19(1)(a). Travel abroad is associated with Article 21, the right to strike is not a Fundamental Right, and clause (f) relating to property has been deleted.
tq: Distinguish implied rights from rights placed under another Article or not recognised as Fundamental Rights.
sec: Article 19(1) clauses (a) to (g), deleted clause (f), freedoms not listed, Articles 19-22  [APPSC]

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The right to protest has been read into the freedom of speech and expression.
2. The right to strike is a Fundamental Right under Article 19(1)(b).
3. Travel abroad is protected under Article 21 and not under Article 19(1)(d).
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. The right to strike is not a Fundamental Right under Article 19(1)(b), although peaceful protest is protected within constitutional limits.
tq: Use the false-right trap by distinguishing protest from strike and domestic movement from foreign travel.
sec: Article 19(1) clauses (a) to (g), deleted clause (f), freedoms not listed, Articles 19-22  [APPSC]

s:
Arrange the following events relating to freedom of speech and expression in chronological order:
A. Decision in Sakal Papers
B. Decision in Romesh Thappar
C. Decision in State of Uttar Pradesh v. Raj Narain
D. Decision in Naveen Jindal
x: Romesh Thappar was decided in 1950, Sakal Papers in 1962, State of Uttar Pradesh v. Raj Narain in 1975, and Naveen Jindal in 2004.
tq: Arrange judicial decisions by their stated years, beginning with the earliest case.
sec: Freedom of speech - implied rights recognised by courts  [APPSC]

s: Which case is associated with the judicial recognition of the right to silence, including the right not to sing the national anthem?
o: Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala
Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India
Cricket Association of Bengal v. Union of India
x: Bijoe Emmanuel (1986) recognised the right to silence, including protection for those who respectfully declined to sing the national anthem.
tq: Match the implied freedom with the distinctive case fact associated with it.
sec: Freedom of speech - implied rights recognised by courts  [APPSC]

s: The right to fly the national flag as an aspect of freedom of expression was recognised in:
x: The Supreme Court recognised the right to fly the national flag in Naveen Jindal (2004) as an aspect of freedom of expression.
tq: Use a distinctive judicially implied right to identify the correct case.
sec: Freedom of speech - implied rights recognised by courts  [APPSC]

s: Commercial speech, including advertisements, was recognised as part of freedom of speech and expression in:
x: The Tata Press decision of 1995 recognised commercial speech, including advertisements, as protected expression under Article 19(1)(a).
tq: Link a specialised form of speech with the case that recognised it.
sec: Freedom of speech - implied rights recognised by courts  [APPSC]

s: Which case recognised speech over the Internet as an aspect of freedom of speech and expression?
x: Anuradha Bhasin (2020) recognised that freedom of speech and expression extends to speech over the Internet.
tq: Use the medium-specific clue to identify the relevant recent constitutional decision.
sec: Freedom of speech - implied rights recognised by courts  [APPSC]

s:
Consider the following statements regarding judicially recognised aspects of Article 19(1)(a):
1. PUCL litigation is associated with safeguards against phone tapping.
2. Cricket Association of Bengal is associated with telecast and the absence of a government monopoly over airwaves.
3. The freedom to demonstrate or picket necessarily includes a Fundamental Right to strike.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. The freedom to demonstrate or picket does not include a Fundamental Right to strike, so statement 3 is false.
tq: Find the overbroad conclusion in a statement that converts a limited protest right into a right to strike.
sec: Freedom of speech - implied rights recognised by courts  [APPSC]

s: Which of the following statements best describes the protection of speech under Article 19?
o: It protects only oral speech made in public places.
It is confined to printed newspapers and books.
It applies only when the communication is not commercial.
It protects speech irrespective of the medium through which it is communicated.
x: Article 19 protects speech and expression irrespective of the medium of communication. Judicial interpretation has extended it to media such as the press, television and the Internet, subject to lawful restrictions.
tq: Apply the broad constitutional principle to different forms of communication rather than limiting it to print.
sec: Freedom of speech - implied rights recognised by courts  [APPSC]

s: Which statement correctly distinguishes films from the press in relation to freedom of speech and expression?
o: Films have no protection under Article 19(1)(a), whereas the press has absolute protection.
Films can be pre-censored in a manner in which the press cannot be pre-censored, partly because films reach larger audiences.
The press can always be pre-censored, whereas films can never be pre-censored.
Neither films nor the press can ever be subject to pre-censorship.
x: Films may be subjected to pre-censorship in a manner in which the press cannot, because films are considered capable of reaching larger audiences. Neither form of expression enjoys absolute protection.
tq: Test the reversed-comparison trap by distinguishing the treatment of films and the press.
sec: Freedom of speech - implied rights recognised by courts  [APPSC]

s:
With reference to Article 19, consider the following statements:
1. Its freedoms are available only to citizens.
2. Foreigners can claim the freedoms under Article 19 in the same manner as citizens.
3. Companies as legal persons cannot themselves claim Article 19 freedoms, although citizen shareholders may sue in appropriate circumstances.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Article 19 rights are available only to citizens; foreigners cannot claim them, and a company as a legal person cannot itself claim them, though citizen shareholders may bring a challenge in appropriate circumstances.
tq: Distinguish citizens, foreigners and legal persons by identifying the category excluded from Article 19.
sec: Article 19 availability - citizens only, foreigners, detained persons  [APPSC]

s: A restriction imposed by a private individual on another person's speech, without any State action, would ordinarily be challenged through:
o: A claim under Article 19(1)(f), which remains enforceable against private persons
An automatic claim under Article 19 against the private individual
An ordinary legal remedy under the applicable law
A claim that Article 19 binds all private persons directly
x: Article 19 primarily protects citizens against State action. A violation by a private person ordinarily requires an ordinary legal remedy under the applicable law, rather than a direct Article 19 claim against that individual.
tq: Ask who is bound by the constitutional right before selecting the available remedy.
sec: Article 19 availability - citizens only, foreigners, detained persons  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following statements regarding a person who is imprisoned or detained is correct?
o: Detention extinguishes every freedom guaranteed by Article 19.
Detention automatically converts Article 19 rights into property rights.
A detained person retains freedom to move throughout India but loses freedom of expression.
A detained person retains freedom of expression, subject to lawful restrictions, even though movement is curtailed.
x: Imprisonment or detention curtails movement but does not by itself extinguish freedom of expression. A detained person may, subject to lawful restrictions, write or publish material such as books.
tq: Separate the specific liberty lost through detention from other freedoms that are not automatically extinguished.
sec: Article 19 availability - citizens only, foreigners, detained persons  [APPSC]

s: Which of the following statements regarding the voters' right to know is correct?
o: It is unrelated to Article 19(1)(a) because voting is not a form of expression.
It includes the voters' right to know about candidates and is linked with Article 19(1)(a).
It is available only to foreign residents of India.
It was created by deleting Article 19(1)(f).
x: The voters' right to know about candidates has been treated as an aspect of freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a). The related material also includes NOTA and ballot secrecy.
tq: Recognise the information-based aspect of electoral participation as an implied expression right.
sec: Freedom of speech - implied rights recognised by courts  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following cases is associated with the striking down of the ban on the journal *Cross Roads* on the ground that 'public order' was not then a constitutionally recognised restriction on free speech?
o: Aveek Sarkar v State of West Bengal
Romesh Thappar v State of Madras
Kedar Nath Singh v State of Bihar
Bennett Coleman v Union of India
x: In Romesh Thappar v State of Madras (1950), the ban on *Cross Roads* was struck down because public order was not then a ground under Article 19(2). The judgment contributed to the First Amendment, 1951.
tq: Use the case-to-ruling association and distinguish the ruling from other speech cases.
sec: Cases on speech and press - ruling or petitioner  [APPSC]

s:
Consider the following pairs:
a. Bennett Coleman v Union of India — Newsprint policy fixing the number of pages violated press freedom
b. Shreya Singhal v Union of India — Section 66A of the Information Technology Act struck down
c. Naveen Jindal case — Flying the national flag recognised as expression under Article 19(1)(a)
d. Aveek Sarkar v State of West Bengal — Community standards test for obscenity
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
x: All four pairs are correctly matched. Bennett Coleman concerned the newsprint policy, Shreya Singhal concerned Section 66A, Naveen Jindal concerned flying the national flag, and Aveek Sarkar adopted the community standards test for obscenity.
tq: Start from the sure case-ruling pairs and verify every pair before selecting the code.
sec: Cases on speech and press - ruling or petitioner  [APPSC]

s: With reference to the freedom of speech and expression, which one of the following statements is correct?
o: Bennett Coleman held that the newsprint policy fixing pages did not affect press freedom.
Bennett Coleman applied the community standards test for obscenity.
Bennett Coleman held that the newsprint policy fixing pages violated press freedom.
Bennett Coleman upheld Section 66A of the Information Technology Act.
x: Bennett Coleman v Union of India (1972) held that the newsprint policy fixing the number of pages violated press freedom.
tq: Discriminate between closely related speech and press cases by identifying the precise subject of the ruling.
sec: Cases on speech and press - ruling or petitioner  [APPSC]

s: Section 66A of the Information Technology Act was struck down by the Supreme Court in:
o: Anuradha Bhasin v Union of India
Kedar Nath Singh v State of Bihar
Kaushal Kishor v State of Uttar Pradesh
Shreya Singhal v Union of India
x: Shreya Singhal v Union of India (2015) struck down Section 66A because it was vague and overbroad.
tq: Match the statutory provision with the case that invalidated it.
sec: Cases on speech and press - ruling or petitioner  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following correctly describes the decision in *Kaushal Kishor v State of Uttar Pradesh* (2023)?
o: Section 66A of the Information Technology Act was upheld subject to safeguards.
The grounds in Article 19(2) are exhaustive and no additional restrictions may be imposed on ministers' speech.
Flying the national flag was held to be outside the protection of Article 19(1)(a).
Public order was held not to be a ground under Article 19(2).
x: Kaushal Kishor held that the grounds in Article 19(2) are exhaustive and that no extra restriction can be imposed on ministers' speech. It also recognised that Articles 19 and 21 can be enforced against non-State actors.
tq: Use the precise holding of the case rather than a broadly related speech-rights proposition.
sec: Cases on speech and press - ruling or petitioner  [APPSC]

s:
Consider the following statements regarding important decisions on speech and communication:
1. Kedar Nath Singh upheld sedition only when connected with incitement to violence or public disorder.
2. Anuradha Bhasin recognised speech and trade over the internet as protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g).
3. Anuradha Bhasin held that internet shutdowns need not be temporary or proportionate if national security is invoked.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Anuradha Bhasin required shutdowns to be proportionate, temporary and published; therefore, statement 3 is incorrect.
tq: Find the statement that reverses the safeguards laid down for restrictions on internet access.
sec: Cases on speech and press - ruling or petitioner  [APPSC]

s: The law replacing the Indian Penal Code came into force on:
x: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita replaced the Indian Penal Code with effect from 1 July 2024.
tq: Test the exact commencement date against nearby constitutional and legal dates.
sec: Cases on speech and press - ruling or petitioner  [APPSC]

s: Which one of the following statements regarding sedition and the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita is correct?
o: Section 66A BNS replaced sedition and criminal defamation.
Section 152 BNS deals with acts endangering the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India, while sedition as Section 124A IPC is gone.
Sedition was retained in the BNS under Section 356.
Section 124A IPC continues unchanged as Section 124A of the BNS.
x: Section 124A IPC, which had been kept in abeyance by the Supreme Court in 2022, is gone under the BNS. Section 152 BNS punishes acts endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity.
tq: Separate the former IPC provision from the new BNS section dealing with sovereignty, unity and integrity.
sec: Cases on speech and press - ruling or petitioner  [APPSC]

s: Criminal defamation, earlier covered by Sections 499 and 500 of the Indian Penal Code, is now dealt with under which provision of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita?
x: Criminal defamation is now covered by Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita; Sections 499 and 500 were the corresponding IPC provisions.
tq: Distinguish the new BNS section for criminal defamation from sections dealing with other speech-related offences.
sec: Cases on speech and press - ruling or petitioner  [APPSC]

s: Which section of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita is identified with hate speech in the stated legal update?
x: Hate speech is identified with Section 196 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita in the stated legal update.
tq: Link the specific offence to its exact statutory section instead of relying on the familiar IPC numbering.
sec: Cases on speech and press - ruling or petitioner  [APPSC]

s: Under Article 19(2), which one of the following is NOT a ground for imposing a reasonable restriction on freedom of speech and expression?
x: General public interest is not a ground listed in Article 19(2). Contempt of court, defamation and incitement to an offence are expressly included.
tq: Find the ground belonging to another Article 19 clause rather than to Article 19(2).
sec: Grounds of reasonable restriction - clauses (2) to (6), grounds added, test of reasonableness  [other exams]

s: Which one of the following is not included among the grounds of restriction under Article 19(2)?
x: Economic grounds are not included in Article 19(2). Sovereignty and integrity, security of the State and friendly relations with foreign States are among the specified grounds.
tq: Reject an attractive but constitutionally unlisted ground by checking the exhaustive list.
sec: Grounds of reasonable restriction - clauses (2) to (6), grounds added, test of reasonableness  [other exams]

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Sedition is expressly listed as a ground under Article 19(2).
2. General public interest is a ground under Article 19(5), but not under Article 19(2).
3. Economic grounds are expressly listed under Article 19(2).
Which of the statements given above is correct?
x: Only statement 2 is correct. Sedition and economic grounds are not listed in Article 19(2), whereas general public interest is a ground under Article 19(5).
tq: Split the options by locating each proposed ground in the correct Article 19 clause.
sec: Grounds of reasonable restriction - clauses (2) to (6), grounds added, test of reasonableness  [other exams]

s:
Which of the following grounds are available for restricting freedom of assembly under Article 19(3)?
1. Sovereignty and integrity of India
2. Public order
3. Morality
4. Security of the State
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
x: Article 19(3) permits restrictions on assembly in the interests of sovereignty and integrity of India and public order. Morality and security of the State are not listed as grounds in Article 19(3).
tq: Use the clause-by-clause comparison to avoid importing grounds from Article 19(2) or 19(4).
sec: Grounds of reasonable restriction - clauses (2) to (6), grounds added, test of reasonableness  [other exams]

s: Freedom of association under Article 19(4) may be reasonably restricted in the interests of:
o: Friendly relations with foreign States, public order, and contempt of court
Security of the State, defamation, and public order
Public order, morality, and sovereignty and integrity of India
General public interest, morality, and professional qualifications
x: Article 19(4) permits restrictions on freedom of association in the interests of sovereignty and integrity of India, public order and morality.
tq: Match the freedom with its own restricted set of grounds rather than using the longer speech list.
sec: Grounds of reasonable restriction - clauses (2) to (6), grounds added, test of reasonableness  [other exams]

s: A restriction on the freedom to move freely throughout India or to reside and settle in any part of India may be imposed under Article 19(5) in the interests of:
o: Security of the State and friendly relations with foreign States
General public interest and protection of the interests of Scheduled Tribes
x: Article 19(5) permits restrictions in the interests of the general public and for protecting the interests of any Scheduled Tribe.
tq: Identify the correct authority of the restriction by matching movement and residence with Article 19(5).
sec: Grounds of reasonable restriction - clauses (2) to (6), grounds added, test of reasonableness  [other exams]

s: Which one of the following is NOT a ground for restricting the freedom to practise any profession or to carry on any occupation, trade or business under Article 19(6)?
o: Protection of the interests of Scheduled Tribes
x: Protection of the interests of Scheduled Tribes is a ground under Article 19(5), relating to movement and residence. Article 19(6) refers to general public interest, professional or technical qualifications, and State trade or monopoly.
tq: Spot the ground borrowed from the neighbouring Article 19(5) provision.
sec: Grounds of reasonable restriction - clauses (2) to (6), grounds added, test of reasonableness  [other exams]

s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below:

List-I (Article 19 clause)
a. Article 19(2)
b. Article 19(3)
c. Article 19(5)
d. Article 19(6)

List-II (Freedom concerned)
i. Movement and residence
ii. Speech and expression
iii. Profession, trade or business
iv. Assembly
x: Article 19(2) concerns speech and expression, Article 19(3) assembly, Article 19(5) movement and residence, and Article 19(6) profession, trade or business.
tq: Start with the familiar clause-freedom pairs and eliminate codes that shift the neighbouring freedoms.
sec: Grounds of reasonable restriction - clauses (2) to (6), grounds added, test of reasonableness  [other exams]

s:
Which of the following grounds were added to Article 19(2) by the First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951?
1. Public order
2. Friendly relations with foreign States
3. Incitement to an offence
4. Sovereignty and integrity of India
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
x: The First Amendment, 1951 added public order, friendly relations with foreign States and incitement to an offence to Article 19(2). Sovereignty and integrity of India was added by the Sixteenth Amendment, 1963.
tq: Separate the grounds added by the First and Sixteenth Amendments instead of treating them as one package.
sec: Grounds of reasonable restriction - clauses (2) to (6), grounds added, test of reasonableness  [other exams]

s: The Sixteenth Constitutional Amendment Act, 1963 added which ground to Articles 19(2), 19(3) and 19(4)?
x: The Sixteenth Amendment, 1963 added sovereignty and integrity of India as a ground in Articles 19(2), 19(3) and 19(4).
tq: Use the amendment-number and year pair to identify the constitutional ground added across three clauses.
sec: Grounds of reasonable restriction - clauses (2) to (6), grounds added, test of reasonableness  [other exams]

s: The State-trade or State-monopoly provision in Article 19(6), which also protects nationalisation, is associated with which Constitutional Amendment?
x: The First Amendment, 1951 added the State-trade clause in Article 19(6), thereby shielding nationalisation from challenge under the freedom of trade and business.
tq: Distinguish the amendment associated with State monopoly from the later amendment associated with sovereignty and integrity.
sec: Grounds of reasonable restriction - clauses (2) to (6), grounds added, test of reasonableness  [other exams]

s:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
A. Decision in *Shreya Singhal v Union of India*
B. First Constitutional Amendment adding public order to Article 19(2)
C. Decision in *Anuradha Bhasin v Union of India*
D. Sixteenth Constitutional Amendment adding sovereignty and integrity of India
x: The correct order is First Amendment (1951), Sixteenth Amendment (1963), Shreya Singhal (2015), and Anuradha Bhasin (2020).
tq: Fix the amendment years first, then place the two later Supreme Court decisions.
sec: Grounds of reasonable restriction - clauses (2) to (6), grounds added, test of reasonableness  [other exams]

s:
In determining whether a restriction on a fundamental right is reasonable, the court considers which of the following factors?
1. Nature of the right
2. Purpose, extent and urgency of the evil
3. Proportionality
4. Whether the restriction completely eclipses the right itself
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
x: The test of reasonableness includes the nature of the right, the purpose, extent and urgency of the evil, and proportionality. A restriction must not eclipse the right itself.
tq: Treat the complete test as cumulative and reject any option that omits a stated factor.
sec: Grounds of reasonable restriction - clauses (2) to (6), grounds added, test of reasonableness  [other exams]

s: The test for determining the reasonableness of restrictions on fundamental rights is particularly associated with which case?
o: Aveek Sarkar v State of West Bengal
State of Madras v V.G. Row
Kaushal Kishor v State of Uttar Pradesh
Romesh Thappar v State of Madras
x: The reasonableness test, involving factors such as the nature of the right, the purpose and urgency of the restriction, and proportionality, is associated with V.G. Row (1952).
tq: Identify the case from the constitutional test rather than from a speech-specific statutory ruling.
sec: Grounds of reasonable restriction - clauses (2) to (6), grounds added, test of reasonableness  [other exams]

s: Which one of the following statements correctly reflects the scope of reasonable restrictions under Article 19?
o: The existence of a restriction removes the need to examine its purpose and urgency.
Once a restriction is enacted in the public interest, the court cannot examine its reasonableness.
Any restriction connected with economic policy automatically satisfies proportionality.
The court determines reasonableness, and a restriction must not destroy or eclipse the right itself.
x: The court decides whether a restriction is reasonable by examining factors including purpose, extent, urgency and proportionality. A restriction must not eclipse the fundamental right itself.
tq: Apply the proportionality principle to distinguish judicial review from unquestioning legislative deference.
sec: Grounds of reasonable restriction - clauses (2) to (6), grounds added, test of reasonableness  [other exams]

s: How many heads of reasonable restriction under Article 19 are counted in the India Year Book 2026 reference?
x: The India Year Book 2026 reference counts 11 heads of reasonable restriction across Article 19.
tq: Test the exact quantitative total rather than inferring it from the number of Article 19 clauses.
sec: Grounds of reasonable restriction - clauses (2) to (6), grounds added, test of reasonableness  [other exams]

s: The year 2026 marks which anniversary of the First Constitutional Amendment?
x: The year 2026 marks 75 years of the First Constitutional Amendment, which was enacted in 1951.
tq: Calculate the anniversary from the amendment year while distinguishing it from the amendment's serial number.
sec: Grounds of reasonable restriction - clauses (2) to (6), grounds added, test of reasonableness  [other exams]

s: Which one of the following is an essential constitutional condition for an assembly protected under Article 19(1)(b)?
o: It must be confined to private premises
It must consist of at least five persons
It must be approved by the Union Government
It must be peaceful and unarmed
x: The freedom to assemble under Article 19(1)(b) protects only peaceful and unarmed assemblies. Violent, disorderly or armed assemblies are outside its protection.
tq: Identify the exact constitutional qualifier and reject broader or substituted conditions.
sec: ■ Freedom of assembly and association - limits (gherao, strikes, arms), co-operatives  [other exams]

s:
Which of the following are included within the freedom of peaceful assembly under Article 19(1)(b)?
1. Meetings
2. Demonstrations
3. Processions
4. Armed gatherings
Select the correct answer using the code below.
x: Meetings, demonstrations and processions may be protected when peaceful and unarmed. Armed gatherings are excluded from the protection.
tq: Separate the protected forms of assembly from the disqualifying condition of being armed.
sec: ■ Freedom of assembly and association - limits (gherao, strikes, arms), co-operatives  [other exams]

s: An assembly held on public land becomes constitutionally unprotected when it is characterised by which of the following?
o: Violence, disorder or possession of arms
Participation by citizens from different States
A demand submitted to the authorities
x: The protection of assembly does not extend to violent, disorderly or armed assemblies. A political objective or inter-State participation by itself does not remove the protection.
tq: Apply the limiting words of the right to a practical situation rather than focusing on the purpose of the assembly.
sec: ■ Freedom of assembly and association - limits (gherao, strikes, arms), co-operatives  [other exams]

s: An assembly of five or more persons may be declared unlawful under which provision as identified in the constitutional law framework?
o: IPC Section 141, corresponding to BNS Section 189
IPC Section 144, corresponding to BNS Section 163
IPC Section 189, corresponding to BNS Section 141
IPC Section 153, corresponding to BNS Section 163
x: The unlawful-assembly provision referred to is IPC Section 141, corresponding to Section 189 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita. Section 144 of the IPC and Section 163 of the BNSS concern prohibitory orders.
tq: Discriminate between the provisions on unlawful assembly and those on prohibitory orders.
sec: ■ Freedom of assembly and association - limits (gherao, strikes, arms), co-operatives  [other exams]

s:
Consider the following statements regarding the right to strike:
1. The right to strike is a Fundamental Right under Article 19.
2. The right to strike is treated as a legal right.
3. A gherao is constitutionally protected as an exercise of peaceful assembly.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: The right to strike is not a Fundamental Right; it is only a legal right. A gherao is not protected as a peaceful assembly.
tq: Test the common confusion between a Fundamental Right and an ordinary legal right.

s: Which case is associated with the proposition that a demonstration may be protected but the right to strike is not a Fundamental Right?
o: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
Kameshwar Prasad v. State of Bihar
T.K. Rangarajan v. State of Tamil Nadu
x: Kameshwar Prasad is identified with the distinction that peaceful demonstration may be protected, whereas the right to strike is not a Fundamental Right.
tq: Match the judicial decision with the specific proposition for which it is cited.

s: With reference to government employees, which one of the following statements is correct?
o: Their right to strike is protected by Article 21 alone.
They possess an unrestricted Fundamental Right to strike.
They may strike whenever a demonstration is peaceful.
They have no right to strike.
x: The decision in T.K. Rangarajan (2003) is cited for the proposition that government employees have no right to strike.
tq: Watch for the authority-specific trap in which a general proposition is incorrectly extended to government employees.

s: The right to form co-operative societies was added to Article 19(1)(c) by which Constitutional Amendment?
x: The Ninety-seventh Amendment Act, 2011 added co-operative societies to the freedom of association under Article 19(1)(c).

s: The right to protest, though not expressly written as a separate freedom, has been read primarily from which provisions?
x: The right to protest is read from freedom of speech and expression, peaceful assembly, and the right to life and personal liberty under Articles 19(1)(a), 19(1)(b) and 21.
tq: Identify the constitutional source provisions rather than looking for a separately named right.

s:
With reference to peaceful protest, consider the following statements:
1. Peaceful protest is recognised as a right of everybody.
2. A protest may occupy public space without restriction because it is peaceful.
3. A protest must not disturb other citizens.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Peaceful protest is recognised as a right, but it cannot occupy public space without limitation or trouble other citizens. Therefore, statements 1 and 3 are correct.
tq: Reject the absolute statement that converts a qualified right into an unrestricted one.

s: The Centre has defended restrictions under the Foreign Contribution Regulation Act in relation to associations by invoking which provision?
x: The Centre has invoked Article 19(4), which concerns reasonable restrictions on the freedom to form associations or unions, in defending FCRA curbs.
tq: Match the restriction clause with the corresponding freedom under Article 19.

s: What was the specific scope of the restriction associated with the INSAF judgment concerning foreign funds?
o: It barred only registered co-operative societies from receiving foreign funds.
It barred all associations from receiving foreign funds.
It removed all restrictions on associations receiving foreign funds.
It barred only bodies in active politics from receiving foreign funds.
x: The INSAF judgment is identified as barring only associations involved in active politics from receiving foreign funds, not all associations.
tq: Watch the scope words “only” and “all” when distinguishing a limited judicial holding from a blanket prohibition.

s: Article 19(1)(d) and Article 19(1)(e) respectively guarantee freedom of:
x: Article 19(1)(d) guarantees movement throughout India, while Article 19(1)(e) guarantees residence and settlement in any part of India.

s: Restrictions on the freedoms under Articles 19(1)(d) and 19(1)(e) may be imposed in the interests of:
o: Only the economic interests of the Union
The general public and the protection of Scheduled Tribes
Only the customs of urban residents
x: Article 19(5) permits reasonable restrictions in the interests of the general public and for protecting the interests of Scheduled Tribes.
tq: Identify both limbs of the constitutional restriction instead of selecting a single-purpose option.

s: Which of the following is an example of a restriction under Article 19(5)?
o: Suspending freedom of speech during every public emergency
Prohibiting all citizens from changing their profession
Preventing all demonstrations on private land
Limiting outsiders' entry and settlement in certain tribal areas
x: Restrictions on outsiders' entry and settlement in tribal or Inner Line areas may protect Scheduled Tribes' culture and land under Article 19(5).
tq: Apply the stated constitutional purpose to the concrete example of tribal and Inner Line areas.

s: The protection of Scheduled Tribes under Article 19(5), in relation to movement and residence, is primarily intended to safeguard their:

s:
Which of the following is authorised by Article 19(6)?
1. Prescribing professional or technical qualifications
2. Carrying on a trade by the State to the exclusion of citizens
3. Creating a State monopoly in a trade
Select the correct answer using the code below.
x: Article 19(6) permits the State to prescribe professional or technical qualifications and to carry on a trade to the exclusion of citizens, thereby permitting State monopolies.
tq: Combine the qualification and State-monopoly limbs instead of treating Article 19(6) as applying to only one of them.

s: The power of the State to prescribe professional or technical qualifications and to create a State monopoly under Article 19(6) was inserted by which Amendment?
x: The relevant provisions of Article 19(6) were inserted by the First Constitutional Amendment.
tq: Match the Article 19 exception with the amendment that inserted it.

s: Which one of the following is NOT protected as an occupation under the freedom of profession, trade or business?
o: A trade conducted under a State monopoly
A dangerous or immoral trade such as trafficking
A lawful profession subject to reasonable regulation
A trade requiring prescribed technical qualifications
x: There is no right to carry on dangerous or immoral trades, such as trafficking. Article 19(6) also permits qualifications and State monopolies.
tq: Find the exception that is inherently outside the protected field rather than merely regulated within it.

s: Article 358 operates automatically when a National Emergency is proclaimed on the ground of:
o: Failure of constitutional machinery in a State
x: Article 358 automatically suspends Article 19 only when the National Emergency is proclaimed on the ground of war or external aggression.
tq: Fix the emergency grounds and reject the broader but constitutionally incorrect alternatives.

s:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 358:
1. It suspends Article 19 automatically during a qualifying National Emergency.
2. It applies when the Emergency is proclaimed on the ground of armed rebellion.
3. After the Forty-fourth Amendment, only laws related to the Emergency receive the relevant protection.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Article 358 operates automatically for an Emergency based on war or external aggression, not armed rebellion. The Forty-fourth Amendment also limited protection to laws related to the Emergency.
tq: Use the amendment-based exception to detect the false emergency ground.
sec: ■ Suspension of Article 19 during emergency - Article 358 condition

s: For which grounds of National Emergency may Article 359 operate, according to the stated constitutional distinction?
o: War, external aggression and armed rebellion
x: Article 359 may operate during an Emergency proclaimed on the ground of war, external aggression or armed rebellion, subject to a Presidential order.
tq: Contrast the three grounds under Article 359 with the narrower grounds under Article 358.
